newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Ortega willing to return seized home.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Ortega willing to return seized home.

text.p: Left-wing Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega on Saturday said he would vacate the house he confiscated during the Nicaraguan revoluion, removing a major roadblock to the reconciliation of the nation's dominant political forces.

"I'm not attached to the house. I'm willing to leave when a solution (to the private property problem) is in sight for all the people," Ortega, who led the 1979-1990 Sandinista government, told Reuters.

The walled-in house, which occupies a city block in Managua, was confiscated from the family of Nicaraguan banker Jaime Morales Carazo by the revolutionary Sandinista government following the 1979 revolution that toppled longtime dictator Anastasio Somoza.

In a scramble before leaving power following their 1990 election loss to former President Violeta Chamorro, the Sandinistas took the titles on some 200,000 properties in what became known as the "Sandinista pinata."

The conflict between the current occupants and the former owners has been a major sticking point in the reconciliation between the Sandinistas and the new government of right-winger Arnoldo Aleman that took office on Jan. 10.
The conflict, symbolised by the dispute over Ortega's house, has also worried foreign investors.
"In Nicaragua we say to visitors, 'My house is your house.' But if you visit Daniel Ortega, he says, 'Your house is my house,'" joked Aleman, whose principal adviser is Morales.
Aleman has said that Ortega must either return the home or pay for it, a demand that until Saturday was flatly rejected by Ortega.

"Comandante Ortega has undergone a total transformation. He has shown himself to be open and ready to resolve the property problem," Aleman said in an unusually warm appraisal of the former revolutionary leader this week.
The condition Ortega put on giving up his house was that those 200,000 families which had been given confiscated properties get other property titles in exchange.

Aleman said his government will give legal property titles to the 200,000 poor families who received confiscated homes, but will demand that wealthy Sandinistas pay for the confiscated property they received.
